blocks.x: The original incarnation of the Batman villain Clayface first appeared in the summer of 1940, with the name Basil Karlo as an homage to a pair of genre-movie actors. That tribute was particularly important because the character was not yet made of clay or in possession of shapeshifting abilities, as he would be in later versions; he was just a B-movie actor using a clay mask to assume the identity of Karlo’s former horror-movie character. Even without the aid of the supernatural, however, Clayface was a natural fit for that year, which saw the release of no fewer than three Universal Monster movies, as sequels to The Invisible Man and The Mummy joined a second wave of monster cinema that would continue for the remainder of the decade.

The new film version of Clayface does not feature a mask-wearing Basil Karlo. Like some of the character’s later iterations in different media, it mixes and matches a few different comics elements, keeping the acting background but using the name Matt Hagen (Tom Rhys Harries) and some mad-science experimentation. But it very much feels of a piece with the Universal horrors that served as sidelong inspiration back in 1940. That year is key; we’re not talking about a James Whale-level monsterpiece like Bride Of Frankenstein or The Invisible Man. But The Invisible Man Returns or The Mummy’s Hand? Sure, Clayface can live up to that.

Hagen has his eye on greater prestige, however. As the movie opens, he’s nervously awaiting news of Oscar nominations (or their DCU equivalent), then basking in his relief and elation upon finding out that he’s among the five Best Actor honorees. When he celebrates in his hometown of Gotham City, however, he accidentally angers gangster Markos Szabo (David Dencik), and receives a facial slashing for his trouble—the first sign that despite a nominally contemporary setting, this movie will be rooted firmly in a pulp world where it’s not only possible for the mafia to slice up a handsome celebrity with impunity, but for the gangsters to somehow plant enough negative rumors in the press that it’s the cracked actor who comes out of the situation looking like the bad guy. (In a nicely noirish touch, it’s never fully specified what those stories about Hagen’s hardscrabble Gotham youth are, or whether they’re actually true. The vague implication is that they probably are.)

After some unsuccessful attempts at reconstructive surgery and a career time-out in Gotham, a heavily scarred Hagen tracks down Caitlyn Corr (Naomie Ackie), a scientist perilously close to losing the funding to experiment with her breakthrough nano-cell technology, which somehow involves using microscopic A.I. to rebuilt damaged tissue. Hagen aggressively volunteers his body to test her work, and despite the potential legal messiness, the prospect of an enthusiastic human subject is too much for her to resist. She’s also drawn to Hagen himself, and the movie makes their maybe-pairing both less likely and less unappealing by handing Caitlyn a working-stiff cop fiancé (Max Minghella), a character with classic (and classically dull) monster-movie functionality.

Broadly, you can probably figure out where and when the tech will appear to work, falter, and/or go overboard, and what kind of powers Hagen will develop as a result. Harries has a distinctive look, and that’s more than half the battle here; he’s handsome, but his impossibly angular face can take hard turns into malevolence before the actual reshaping begins. To convey that process beyond the initial drips and droops, director James Watkins wisely relies on tricky cuts more often than computerized morphing effects; when he depicts the transition through shadows cast on a wall, even better! The eventual addition of CG morphs mostly serve as a reminder of how good the graphics in Terminator 2 still look all these years later.

Clayface is a lower-budget affair than that blockbuster, or just about any live-action Batman-related movies from the past 40 years—which also means that it can’t afford anything like Burton-style architectural grandeur or even Schumacher-style mega-chintz, despite featuring the most fantastical Batman bad guy to be portrayed in live-action since Mr. Freeze and Poison Ivy teamed up for an evil plot to ruin the series. Gels, however, are plenty affordable, so the movie has plenty of red glow, along with orange-yellow interiors, neon-streaked streets, and the pervasive backlighting that has oddly become a DCU signature. Gotham is still missing the sense of place that left with Christopher Nolan, but for now it’s a workable B-movie milieu. It will probably need an upgrade if the DCU really grows its own new Batman series, but that’s well above this movie’s pay grade, and ours.

Best to meet Clayface on its own terms. In the tradition of those mid-tier Universal Monsters sequels, it ultimately feels a little workmanlike, especially regarding its barely there body horror. (Was it more prominent in the original Mike Flanagan screenplay, reworked by at least one other writer?) Though there are some appropriately skin-crawling images of bodily malleability, Hagen’s fear for the life and career he thought he was about to get is more practical than visceral. Harries conveys the actor’s ego but not the pure horror he should feel about his moneymaking face turned against him—or looking in the mirror and seeing other faces stare back at him. But then, body horror as we think of it today wasn’t really around in 1940, either.

The more important contemporary comparison probably wouldn’t be The Substance but rather those movies in the Spidey Universe Of Cinematic Killers at Sony. The company would repeatedly tee up monstrous Spider-Man villains only to immediately back away and reconceive them as antiheroes with essentially decent hearts. Watkins and Flanagan have far too much sense to pull any of that here; Hagen’s Clayface makes for a pitiable creature and sometimes a deliciously wicked one, as in a set piece where he infiltrates a gangster nightclub. But he’s not here to do the right thing. Like a classic monster, his unusual physique and his human weaknesses team up to foster his ultimate alienation.
Starring: Tom Rhys Harries, Naomie Ackie, David Dencik, Max Minghella
